text: A fellow critic made a post about the lack of sincerity in modern movies. From about 2016 onward, many major releases have had a problem of undercutting themselves with self-referential jabs and not taking their characters, ideas, or stories seriously. As such, one of my goals for 2026 is to see more movies from decades past. Classics I haven’t gotten to yet, older movies I was recommended but put off, etc. Sincerity in movies, regardless of genre, is what makes them worth watching in the first place, and I want more of that. So I’m unofficially naming 2026 my “year of sincere”. I’m looking forward to challenging myself with this and recommending more good films to y’all. Happy watching!

text: The Galaxy Far Far Away has new creative leadership. Longtime Star Wars producer Dave Filoni and visual effects artist and ILM executive vice president Lynwen Brennan have reportedly been tapped by The Force to oversee LucasFilm and the Star Wars franchise. Star Wars has been through a rough patch over the last decade or so with various projects announced only to be pulled or significantly reworked, and while I’ve enjoyed some of its output (“The Force Awakens”, “Rogue One”, and “Solo”), overall the franchise’s uncertainty in both direction and target audience has been frustrating. Hopefully Brennan and Filoni can keep what works, shepherd more consistency and variety across projects, and re-engage old fans while bringing in new ones.

text: While its first act is front-loaded with cringey buzzwords, “Prom Pact” soon reveals itself as a sweet, funny, and well-executed teen movie with sincerity for its characters. Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Milo Manheim are perfectly cast, Margaret Cho is hilarious, and I love its handling of not judging books by their covers, smart use of ‘80s references, and surprisingly believable employment of teen tropes. I wish I liked its start more, but if you like teen movies, accept this proposal. 3.5/5. See it on DisneyPlus!

text: I’ve been on here less recently and it’s doing me good. This place and especially Threads can be cesspools of negativity sometimes and I see more posts complaining about how “all modern movies are slop” or “feel like they were written by AI” than celebrating films they love or offering mature critiques and discussions of the ones they don’t. I’ve never been shy about when a film or show grinds my gears, but at the end of the day, regardless of my feelings on it, I respect the effort of everyone who made it. Praise the films you love, criticize the ones you don’t, but every one of them worth discussing, good or bad, was made by people.

text: I think part of the reason why younger people today aren’t as interested in black-and-white films (or movies past a certain decade) is because they grew up constantly hearing about how “problematic” older movies are, that they “don’t hold up to modern attitudes” over the late 2010s. It’s good to acknowledge elements of an older movie that haven’t aged well for you, but if the goal is to encourage more young film lovers to see older movies and how they shaped the landscape of today, focus more on the strengths of those films in discussion than their dated weaknesses when telling film fans why they should see them.

text: The difference between a good and bad unlikable character is whether or not that unlikability is intentional or not. Good unlikable characters can be the ones I love to hate or am fascinated to follow to despite their failings, but the story still recognizes their unlikability. Bad unlikable characters are the ones that a story fails to recognize are unlikable and operate as if I like them even when their actions lead me to feel otherwise.

text: “The Bride!” Is a dark, campy romance spin on Frankenstein that understands and respects Mary Shelley’s themes while weaving a story all its own. Jessie Buckley, Christian Bale, and Penelope Cruz are in fine form, Maggie Gyllenhaal’s direction and navigation between tones is confident, and even though some story elements go underexplored, it’s a good time if you can ride its weird wavelength. It won’t be for everyone, but this came alive for me. 3.5/5. See it if yuu like weird stuff.

text: The “Buffy” continuation has been canned at Hulu, per Sarah Michelle Gellar. While there’s a lot of speculation around why the cancellation occurred, I have mixed feelings about it. On one hand, I’d love to see the story continue with a new Slayer whose adventures could make new horror fans like the original show did for me. On the other hand, I’ve seen many attempted continuations lack what made their originals special and wouldn’t want “Buffy” on that list. Whatever happens in the future, I’m glad the original run will be around for new generations to sink their stakes into.

text: “Batman V Superman: Dawn of Justice” is 10 years old today. There are small things I enjoy about it and big things I don’t that I’ll forever question how they made it to screen, but without it, I probably wouldn’t have gotten several superhero films I enjoy that were made in reaction to it. The “Wonder Woman”, “Shazam!”, and “Aquaman” duologies, “The Suicide Squad”, “Birds of Prey”, and the newest “Superman” wouldn’t be the movies they are if “BVS” hadn’t been what it was. So I wish “BVS” a happy 10-year anniversary thankful for the movies it led to. Happy birthday to it.

text: Something i love about “Contact” is how it takes Jodie Foster’s Ellie Arroway, a scientist and skeptic who doesn’t understand people who believe in God based on their faith despite any tangible proof of his existence, and climaxes with her pleading with another skeptic to believe in something else extraordinary despite her having no tangible proof that what she experienced was real. The film’s ambiguousness about what really happened is a strength, but I like how it puts her in the very scenario she’s been scoffing at over the story and, to me at least, leads her to truly understand what it’s like being in the opposite end of the argument.
